title: Mathlib Imports
content: Imports Mathlib tactics, real number basics, finite sets, and affine space. The affine space import provides the geometric foundation, while finite sets are used for counting distinct circles via Finset.card on images of triple products.
mathContext: Requires $\text{Fin}\,2 \to \mathbb{R}$ for $\mathbb{R}^2$ points, $\text{Finset.card}$ for circle counting, and $\text{Finset.image}$ for mapping triples to circumcircles.

title: Points and Collinearity
content: Point2 is $\mathbb{R}^2$ represented as $\text{Fin}\,2 \to \mathbb{R}$. Collinearity of three points $p, q, r$ is detected by the vanishing of the cross product $(q_x - p_x)(r_y - p_y) - (r_x - p_x)(q_y - p_y) = 0$, which is the signed area criterion for the triangle $pqr$.
mathContext: $\text{AreCollinear}(p, q, r) \iff (q_x - p_x)(r_y - p_y) = (r_x - p_x)(q_y - p_y)$, i.e., the $2 \times 2$ determinant vanishes

title: Circumcircle Construction
content: Three non-collinear points uniquely determine a circle (their circumcircle). The center is computed as the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of two sides of the triangle $pqr$, using the standard formula involving the $2 \times 2$ determinant $d = 2(a_x(b_y - c_y) + b_x(c_y - a_y) + c_x(a_y - b_y))$. The SameCircle predicate identifies triples that define the same circumcircle, enabling distinct circle counting.
mathContext: Center: $(u_x, u_y)$ with $u_x = \frac{(a_x^2+a_y^2)(b_y-c_y) + \cdots}{d}$; two triples are equivalent iff $(\text{center}, r^2)$ agree

title: Point Configurations and Degeneracy
content: PointConfig n is an indexed family of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. AllConcyclic requires all points to lie on a single circle (common center and radius), while AllCollinear requires all triples to be collinear. These are the two degeneracy conditions excluded in the problem: concyclic points determine only 1 circle, and collinear points determine no circles.
mathContext: $\text{AllConcyclic} \iff \exists (c, r),\; \forall i,\; \|p_i - c\|^2 = r^2$; $\text{AllCollinear} \iff \forall i,j,k,\; \text{AreCollinear}(p_i, p_j, p_k)$

title: Circle Counting
content: numCircles counts distinct circles by mapping all triples $(i,j,k)$ of point indices to their circumcircle (center, $r^2$) pair and taking the cardinality of the image. This counts each geometric circle once regardless of how many triples define it. A set of $n$ points produces at most $\binom{n}{3}$ triples but potentially far fewer distinct circles. The minCircles function (though simplified in the formalization) represents the extremal quantity $f(n)$.

title: Elliott's Theorem (1967)
content: P.D.T.A. Elliott proved that for $n > 393$ points in general position (not all concyclic, not all collinear), the number of distinct circles is at least $\binom{n-1}{2} = (n-1)(n-2)/2$. The bound is tight: $n$ points distributed on two concentric circles achieve it. Elliott's proof uses an inductive argument on point deletion, analyzing how removing a point affects the circle count. The threshold $n > 393$ comes from the induction base.

title: Segre's Cube Projection Counterexample
content: Beniamino Segre showed that projecting the 8 vertices of a cube onto a suitable plane produces 8 points that are neither concyclic nor collinear but determine fewer than $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ distinct circles. This demonstrates that Elliott's lower bound $\binom{n-1}{2}$ cannot hold for all $n$, specifically failing at $n = 8$. The cube's high symmetry group (order 48) forces many triples to share circumcircles.
